hits.name: Guillermo Rauch
hits.text:
At @vercel we got to test this model before release. Best way to summarize it: astonishingly brilliant.

One interesting takeaway: it's very clear that this new generation of models can take on unprecedented bodies of parallel work.

To actually seize this intelligence, you need cloud sandboxes. Full stop. The model can delegate and orchestrate far more than a single computer can handle. Likely far more than you can even imagine it can handle.

Your bottleneck is now ① your ambition and ② your parallel computing power.

Btw, I learned from @cramforce you don't need to overcomplicate it. Install Vercel CLI, setup the Plugin and tell the agent to use /𝚘𝚏𝚏𝚕𝚘𝚊𝚍-𝚝𝚘-𝚜𝚊𝚗𝚍𝚋𝚘𝚡 skill. It'll provision and de-allocate cloud sandboxes as needed. You don't need a "multi-agent remote harness ralph orchestrator" 😆

hits.name: Guillermo Rauch
hits.text:
So bullish on MCP. Its utility exceeds the "M" part: even AI aside, it'll be a civilization-scale accomplishment to get all our systems communicating through one universal open protocol.

A missing piece was how to get arbitrary callbacks across sessions. MCP could read and write, but it couldn't tell you later "this event happened." MCP Events fixes this.

We're adding support in our own MCP. Say an agent makes a deployment, and wants to know when it's complete. Instead of polling, it can subscribe to 𝚍𝚎𝚙𝚕𝚘𝚢𝚖𝚎𝚗𝚝.𝚜𝚞𝚌𝚌𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚎𝚍.

PSA: With Vercel Queues and Workflows, writing the backend machinery for your own MCPs to do this is easy peasy.

hits.name: Ethan Mollick
hits.text:
A favorite optimistic view of the future of AI is from a pessimistic book that not about AI: "Rise and Fall of American Growth," which argues that we had a one-time explosion in living standards from 1870 and 1920 (& later outside the US).

In 1870: no toilets, no city plumbing, lamp light, no central heating, little public health, horses for local travel, etc. In 50 years, all of this was solved & the nation was electrified. In the next fifty modern medicine, air travel and telecommunication happened.

The book then points out that we have had no changes in lifestyle of similar scale since the 1970s. Written in 2016, it argued that we would likely never experience another boom like the "Special Century." The positive view of AI should make us ask "But what if we do?" and "How do we make it all go right?"

hits.name: elvis
hits.text:
Must-read paper on scaling multi-agent swarms.

The main focus right now is training agent swarms to coordinate and cooperate better. Here is a promising new work on this.

The problem:

Multi-agent systems usually follow a plan that a developer writes ahead of time.

The plan decides which agent does what and when agents message each other, and it usually stays the same across tasks.

What they propose:

s3 has the agents learn that plan instead. Agents learn through cooperative RL when to work alone, when to share findings, and when to read teammates' work. There are no predefined roles.

With matched training and inference budgets, s3 swarms tested at twice their training size solve over 25x more coordination problems than the strongest baseline. In parallel exploration, communicating agents repeat nearly 50% less work and beat best-of-N by up to 9.4 points.

The agents develop complementary roles on their own, and those roles carry over to bigger teams.

https://t.co/uqGIs6ZACo

Chat with Paper: https://t.co/WtMRctTYSe

hits.name: Kai
hits.text:
🚨 Claude Code's "Don't Ask Again" feature could accidentally expose your passwords on GitHub.

Security firm Apiiro found publicly exposed Claude Code config files on GitHub containing database passwords, API keys, and even SSH login keys.

Here's how it happens.

Say you ask Claude Code to connect to a database using a command that includes your password.

When you click "Yes, and don't ask again", Claude Code may save the entire command to .claude/settings.local.json, including the password.

If that file gets pushed to a public GitHub repo, your password goes with it.

Claude Code normally tries to keep this file out of Git, but that protection can fail if the file is already being tracked.

Worth checking your .claude/settings.local.json and Git history.

If any credentials have been exposed, rotate them. Just deleting the file isn't enough, since the secrets may still be in Git history.
